title: Secure Defaults and Defensive Design
learningObjectives: Explain the core ideas and terminology of secure defaults and defensive design.
Recognize the risks or mistakes this topic is intended to prevent.
Apply appropriate defensive practices in a beginner project.
Distinguish this topic from related security concepts and controls.
Review a simple design and justify improvements using evidence.

understand.concept: Secure defaults make the safer choice automatic: deny access unless allowed, use protected transport, limit permissions, avoid exposing data, and require explicit opt-in for risky actions. Defensive design anticipates invalid states, failures, and misuse. Convenience should not silently weaken protections, and security controls should be clear, testable, and consistent.
understand.whyItMatters: Users and maintainers often keep defaults; safer defaults protect people who do not know every setting.
understand.analogy: Think of a careful community space where entry, use of shared items, and privacy are guided by clear rules and appropriate checks.
understand.analogyLimit: Software security depends on technical boundaries, data flows, implementation details, and changing threats that this analogy cannot fully represent.

explain.narrative:
Secure defaults make the safer choice automatic: deny access unless allowed, use protected transport, limit permissions, avoid exposing data, and require explicit opt-in for risky actions. Defensive design anticipates invalid states, failures, and misuse. Convenience should not silently weaken protections, and security controls should be clear, testable, and consistent.

Apply these principles proportionately. Use established platform and library protections instead of improvising security-critical mechanisms. For a real application, confirm requirements and review the implementation with qualified peers.

examples.title: Default to denial
examples.explanation: An unknown permission state does not grant access.

examples.title: Require explicit opt-in
examples.code:
const enabled = false;
console.log(enabled ? 'enabled' : 'disabled by default');
examples.explanation: Risky features should not be enabled silently.

examples.title: Bound an operation
examples.explanation: Bounds help prevent unexpected resource use in this simple example.

examples.title: Handle missing values
examples.explanation: A defined fallback prevents unclear behavior.

examples.title: Make a check visible
examples.explanation: Failing a required check should be visible, not ignored.

commonMistakes: Assuming a feature is safe because it works in normal use.
Trusting client-side controls as the only enforcement.
Applying one generic transformation to every kind of input or output.
Exposing credentials or personal data in source, logs, or screenshots.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Design a secure-default checklist for a beginner web app. Include access, configuration, transport, privacy, limits, recovery, and testing. Provide a rationale for each default.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy project and no real secrets or personal data.
Design a secure-default checklist for a beginner web app. Include access, configuration, transport, privacy, limits, recovery, and testing. Provide a rationale for each default.
Explain the decisions you made and limitations.
Identify at least one test or review step.

hints: If permission is unknown, do not grant it.
Make limits and safe fallbacks explicit.
Test failure and misuse cases, not only happy paths.
